hits.text: In the fault detection step, we use two approaches: (a) agents enabled with classical machine learning techniques and (b) agents and critics enabled with Generative AI’s foundation models. In the Severity and Cause analysis step, we use agents and critics enabled with Generative AI’s foundation models. In classical machine learning, the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XG Boosting) model is used; it provides higher accuracy, F1 score, precision, and recall with faster processing than Generative AI’s foundation models in the fault detection phase. In classical machine learning based approach, agents are enabled with the Extreme Gradient Boosting model; however, critics are not used (it does not affect the model formulation). Nevertheless, we use both agents and critics in the Generative AI’s foundation model-based approaches for fault detection. In the fault detection step, we can use agents enabled with foundation models, and then critics enabled with the XG Boosting or vice versa, but at the cost of higher execution time. One of the advantages of enabling agents with classical machine learning is the speed and accuracy of fault detection, which is crucial in segregating the faults faster. For fault severity and cause analysis, we use agents and critics enabled by foundation models. The developed model is suitable for real-time fault detection, severity, and cause analysis. We make the following principal contributions to the paper.

hits.text: Using the time duration of fault events presented in the event file of the dataset 4 of [ 15 ] , we extract the fault data and add a fault column in the CSV file. An equal number of no-fault entries is added to the CSV file; the entries are labeled as “1” for fault and “0” for no fault, we call the dataset a balanced dataset . Furthermore, these entries are randomized. Fault detector agents enabled with the XG Boosting: For the XG Boosting, the balanced dataset with fault column (CSV file) is split into two parts—one is used for training and another for testing purposes. XG Boosting model is trained with 2/3 of the records, and the remaining records (test files) are split into smaller files. The XG Boosting trained model is saved and accessed by fault detector agents. At each iteration, active agents access a CSV test file to predict the faults. The resulting fault-classified data is saved as a CSV file. Fault detector agents and critics enabled with large language models (LLMs): AI agents and critics can access different large language models (LLMs), such as Llama3.2, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral, etc., for response generation and evaluation. For LLM-enabled agents and critics, the CSV data are converted into text queries and saved as CSV files for efficient processing by the LLMs. For the fault detection step with LLM-enabled agents and critics, the text queries CSV file is then converted into smaller chunks to pass to agents and critics for fault detection. At each iteration, an active agent processes a file and passes its responses to critics for feedback. An active critic then evaluates the agent’s responses, checks their correctness, and sends feedback to the agent

hits.text: . Recall that in the fault detection step with the XG Boosting, the fault-classified data is saved in CSV files, which are converted into text queries with predicted faults as a column. Whereas, for LLM-enabled fault detection, the CSV network telemetry data is pre-processed to create text queries and accessed by agents and critics to predict faults (‘Fault’, ‘No Fault’), the predicted value is added as a column in the queries and saved as CSV files. The queries with predicted ‘Fault’ are saved in another CSV files based on processed query chunks. These query data files are accessible to AI agents for fault severity and cause analysis. The AI agents first classify the faults as ‘Critical’ or ‘Non-critical’ with access to the network telemetry log files (stored in ChromaDB) and provide a brief cause of the fault. The AI agent’s response is then sent to AI critics for evaluation. An active critic evaluates the correctness of the agent’s fault severity classification and cause summary and sends feedback to the agent for further improvement. The critics also have access to network telemetry log files through ChromaDB instances. After receiving the feedback, the agent improves its response. The responses are saved in CSV files. The ‘Critical’ flagged faults can be notified to network administrator.

hits.text: We evaluate our model with an open-source network telemetry dataset available at [ 15 ] for fault detection, severity, and cause analysis. We chose dataset 4 that contains tabular data in a comma-separated values (CSV) format and log files for port state changes. The data has three types of port state changes: Optical transceiver pull and reinsert, admin state change (down and up), and link state changes (plug-in and plug-out of fiber optics cable). For fault detection, developed model is evaluated by two approaches: AI agents enabled with classical machine learning techniques (e.g., XG Boosting), and AI agents and critics enabled with large language models. We observe that agents enabled with XG Boosting provide faster results and higher accuracy, F1-score, precision, and recall than AI agents and critics enabled with LLMs. As described earlier, the CSV file of network telemetry dataset 4 of [ 15 ] has 99 columns, which include numeric and non-numeric data. Data are pre-processed before being accessible to AI agents and critics. The pre-processing step is presented in the following subsection.
